cards.meaning: large enough to matter
cards.example: The new process saved a substantial amount of time.
cards.note: More formal than 'big' or 'a lot of'.

cards.meaning: real but not obvious at first
cards.example: The underlying problem was poor communication between teams, not the software.
cards.note: Comes before a noun.

cards.meaning: a likely result or meaning that is not said directly
cards.example: The implications of the budget cut are still unclear.
cards.note: Say 'implications for' someone or something.

cards.meaning: something that limits what you can do
cards.example: Time was our main constraint, so we dropped the second survey.
cards.note: Often plural: 'under financial constraints'.

cards.meaning: possible and practical to do
cards.example: A full redesign is not feasible before March.
cards.note: A formal word for 'doable'.

cards.meaning: strong and reliable; hard to break or prove wrong
cards.example: We need more robust data before we change the policy.

cards.meaning: very small; hardly important
cards.example: The change made only a marginal difference to sales.
cards.note: The opposite of 'substantial'.

cards.meaning: to make something bad less serious
cards.example: We mitigated the risk by testing with a small group first.
cards.note: Formal. The object is the bad thing: 'mitigate the damage'.

cards.meaning: it is possible to argue that; a careful way to give a strong opinion
cards.example: This is arguably the most important decision the team has made this year.
cards.note: Softer than stating the opinion as a fact.

cards.meaning: to show or suggest
cards.example: Early results indicate a small rise in demand.
cards.note: 'Indicate' and 'suggest' leave room for doubt; 'prove' does not.

cards.meaning: short and clear, with no extra words
cards.example: Please keep the summary concise, one page at most.

cards.meaning: to say that something is caused by something else
cards.example: We attribute the drop in complaints to the new training.
cards.note: As a verb the stress is on the second syllable: at-TRIB-ute.

cards.meaning: including everything or nearly everything
cards.example: The report gives a comprehensive review of our suppliers.

cards.meaning: a difference between things that should match
cards.example: There is a discrepancy between the two sets of figures.

cards.meaning: the information suggests this, but I am not certain
cards.example: It appears that the delay was caused by a supplier.
cards.note: More formal than 'it looks like'.

cards.meaning: usually do; happen often but not always
cards.example: Smaller teams tend to make decisions faster.
cards.note: Turns an absolute claim into a fair general one.

cards.meaning: will probably
cards.example: The new rules are likely to increase costs slightly.

cards.meaning: it is almost certain that
cards.example: There is little doubt that the training improved staff confidence.
cards.note: Strong, but leaves a small door open. 'No doubt' is stronger.

cards.meaning: partly, not completely
cards.example: To some extent, the problem was our own planning.

cards.meaning: however, after what I have just said
cards.example: The trial was a success. That said, it was very small.
cards.note: Starts a new sentence and limits the point that came before.

cards.meaning: showing a clear difference from what was just said
cards.example: Sales in the north rose. By contrast, the south stayed flat.

cards.meaning: I will say the same thing more simply or practically
cards.example: We are over budget. To put it another way, we cannot hire anyone else this year.

cards.meaning: because of; taking this into account
cards.example: In light of the feedback, we have changed the schedule.
cards.note: 'In the light of' is also common in British English.

cards.meaning: about; on the subject of
cards.example: With regard to the budget, there is no change.
cards.note: Formal. In speech, 'as for' or 'about' sounds more natural.

cards.meaning: in short; here are the main points
cards.example: To sum up, the plan is feasible but needs more staff.

cards.meaning: first I will explain the situation
cards.example: To give you some context, the team had lost two people that spring.
cards.note: A good opening for the Situation step of a STAR answer.

cards.meaning: this was my job in that situation
cards.example: My role was to rebuild trust with the client.
cards.note: The Task step of STAR: say what you were responsible for.

cards.meaning: because of this
cards.example: As a result, response times fell by a third.
cards.note: The Result step of STAR: give a number or a clear change when you can.

cards.meaning: my view, which I can support, is that
cards.example: I would argue that the delay saved us money in the long run.
cards.note: Firm but open to discussion.

cards.meaning: you are very welcome to (formal)
cards.example: Please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any questions.
cards.note: Formal writing. Informal equivalents: 'just let me know' or 'give me a shout'.

cards.meaning: looking back, knowing what I know now
cards.example: With hindsight, I would have involved the client earlier.
cards.note: Shows that you learn from experience.

cards.meaning: I accept that your question is reasonable, and I will answer it
cards.example: That's a fair question. The project did go over budget, and here is why.
cards.note: Gives you a moment to think. A plain pause before answering works too.

cards.meaning: puts your main point at the end, where it gets attention
cards.example: What we need is a clearer plan.
cards.note: The what-clause counts as one thing, so the verb is usually 'is'.

cards.meaning: points at one part of the sentence as the important one
cards.example: It was the second interview that changed my mind.
cards.note: Use 'It is' for the present: 'It is the cost that worries us.'

cards.meaning: gives a cause clearly and formally
cards.example: The reason the project stalled is that nobody owned it.
cards.note: In formal English say 'the reason is that', not 'the reason is because'.

cards.meaning: only this, nothing more
cards.example: All we need is another week.
cards.note: 'All' here means 'the only thing'.

cards.meaning: turns an action into a noun so it can be the subject
cards.example: The introduction of online booking has reduced waiting times.
cards.note: Nominalisation makes writing compact and formal. Use it in reports, not in chat.

cards.meaning: links a change to its result, using nouns
cards.example: The rise in prices led to a fall in demand.
cards.note: Say 'a rise in prices', not 'a rise of prices'.

cards.meaning: says how strong the support for a claim is
cards.example: There is growing evidence that short breaks improve focus.
cards.note: 'Evidence' is uncountable: not 'an evidence' or 'evidences'.

cards.meaning: admits that something is probably true, then adds your point
cards.example: The plan may well be cheaper, but it carries more risk.
cards.note: 'Well' makes 'may' more likely, not less.

cards.meaning: puts two contrasting facts in one sentence
cards.example: While the first quarter was strong, the second was disappointing.

cards.meaning: one action finished before the next, done by the same people
cards.example: Having reviewed the data, we decided to extend the trial.
cards.note: Both parts must have the same subject.

lessons.title: The vocabulary of careful work
lessons.why: Precise words let you say exactly how big, how possible or how serious something is, so people trust what you tell them.

passage.title: Briefing note: moving the help desk online
passage.text:
Purpose: to set out whether moving the help desk online by June is feasible.

The main constraint is staff time. Two of our five advisers are already working on the new billing system, so any plan has to work within that limit. A complete move in one step is therefore not feasible. A phased move, starting with password resets, is.

The pilot in Leeds gave us robust figures: over three months, 40 per cent of simple requests were handled online, which is a substantial saving. The gain for complex requests was marginal, and we do not expect that to change.

The underlying issue is not technology but habit. Many callers phone because they always have. The implication for us is that the online service must be easier than the phone, not merely available.

Two risks remain: some older users may feel shut out, and advisers may worry about their jobs. We can mitigate both by keeping a phone line for anyone who wants it and by involving advisers in the design from the start.

Recommendation: approve a phased move, beginning in April.

drills.prompt: A change saved the team 40 per cent of their time. Which word describes that saving?
drills.hint: Forty per cent is a lot.
drills.why: 'Substantial' means large enough to matter. 'Marginal' means very small, and 'feasible' is about whether something can be done at all.

drills.sentence: A full redesign is not ___ with two people and six weeks.
drills.hint: The sentence is about whether it can be done.
drills.why: 'Feasible' means possible and practical. 'Robust' describes strength or reliability, and 'underlying' comes before a noun.

drills.sentence: We can ___ the risk by testing the change on a small group first.
drills.hint: Which verb means 'make a bad thing less serious'?
drills.why: You mitigate a risk. You attribute a result to a cause, and results indicate something.

drills.sentence: The change made a substantial difference: sales rose by 0.2 per cent.
drills.answer: The change made a marginal difference: sales rose by 0.2 per cent.
accept: The change made only a marginal difference: sales rose by 0.2 per cent.
The change made a small difference: sales rose by 0.2 per cent.
drills.hint: Does 0.2 per cent sound large?
drills.why: 0.2 per cent is tiny, so 'substantial' misleads the reader. 'Marginal' matches the number.

drills.answer: What are the implications for our team?
drills.hint: Start with the question word.
drills.why: We talk about the implications 'for' someone or something.

parts: The data comes from one small pilot.
We should not treat it as robust.
answers: Because the data comes from one small pilot, we should not treat it as robust.
The data comes from one small pilot, so we should not treat it as robust.
Since the data comes from one small pilot, we should not treat it as robust.
drills.hint: Show the reason and the result in one sentence.
drills.why: 'Because' or 'since' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result. Either way the reader sees why the data is weak.

drills.prompt: Which sentence fits a formal report?
options: Doing it all at once just isn't doable.
A single-stage transition is not feasible.
No way we can do it all in one go.
drills.hint: Look for the formal word from this lesson.
drills.why: 'Feasible' and 'transition' belong to formal writing. The other two are fine with a colleague but too casual for a report.

write.prompt: Write a short briefing note to a manager about a change you would like to make at work or in your studies. Say whether it is feasible, name the main constraint and the underlying problem it solves, say how substantial the benefit would be, and describe one risk and how you would mitigate it.

speak.prompt: A colleague asks whether a change you want is realistic. Explain the main constraint, how substantial the benefit is, and how you would mitigate one risk. Take your time: stopping to choose the exact word is part of speaking precisely.

lessons.check: What is the difference between a substantial benefit and a marginal one? Give an example of each from your own work or studies.

lessons.title: How sure are you? Hedging and certainty
lessons.why: Saying exactly how sure you are makes you credible: overclaiming loses trust, and too much doubt hides your point.

passage.title: Research summary: remote meetings and decisions
passage.text:
This summary reports on a staff survey (412 responses) and a review of meeting records from the past year.

There is little doubt that remote meetings have become shorter: the records show an average fall from 52 to 38 minutes. What is less clear is whether they have become better.

The survey responses indicate that people who join remotely tend to speak less, particularly in larger meetings. It appears that this is not a matter of confidence alone; several respondents mentioned poor sound and the difficulty of finding a moment to come in.

There is limited evidence that decisions made in remote meetings are reversed more often. The numbers are small, so this finding should be treated with caution. To some extent, it may reflect the kind of decisions that are made remotely rather than the format itself.

Taken together, the findings suggest that shorter meetings are likely to stay, and that chairs will need to invite remote participants in more deliberately. This is arguably the most practical change the organisation can make, and it costs nothing.

drills.prompt: Your data comes from one small survey. Which sentence claims the right amount?
options: The survey proves that staff prefer remote work.
The survey suggests that many staff prefer remote work.
Everyone knows that staff prefer remote work.
drills.hint: How much can one small survey show?
drills.why: One small survey can suggest, not prove. 'Proves' overclaims, and 'everyone knows' gives no evidence at all.

drills.prompt: Which sentence is the most certain?
options: It appears that costs will rise.
There is little doubt that costs will rise.
drills.hint: One of these means 'almost certain'.
drills.why: 'There is little doubt that' means almost certain. 'Likely' means probable, and 'it appears' and 'may' are weaker still.

drills.sentence: Younger users ___ to prefer the app, although many older users like it too.
drills.hint: Which verb means 'usually, but not always' and is followed by 'to'?
drills.why: 'Tend to' describes what usually happens. 'Indicate' and 'suggest' are not followed by 'to' plus a verb.

drills.sentence: There is little ___ that the training helped: every team improved.
drills.hint: Every team improved, so the writer is very sure.
drills.why: 'There is little doubt' means almost certain, which fits. 'Little evidence' or 'little chance' would say the opposite of the second half.

drills.sentence: There is strong evidence that the new timetable reduced complaints, although we only have two weeks of data.
drills.answer: There is limited evidence that the new timetable reduced complaints, although we only have two weeks of data.
accept: There is some evidence that the new timetable reduced complaints, although we only have two weeks of data.
drills.hint: Can two weeks of data be strong evidence?
drills.why: The sentence contradicts itself. Two weeks of data gives limited or some evidence, so the hedge must match.

drills.answer: It appears that the supplier was at fault.
drills.hint: Begin with the hedge, then the claim.
drills.why: 'It appears that' introduces a conclusion you are fairly, but not fully, sure of.

answers: While the results are encouraging, the sample was small.
Although the results are encouraging, the sample was small.
The results are encouraging, although the sample was small.
The results are encouraging; that said, the sample was small.
drills.hint: Keep both ideas and show the contrast.
drills.why: A careful writer gives the good news and its limit together, so the reader does not overestimate the finding.

write.prompt: Write a short research summary on something you have noticed at work, in your studies or in the news. Use at least four ways of showing how sure you are, from 'there is little doubt that' to 'it appears that', and make each one match the strength of your evidence.

speak.prompt: A colleague asks what you think will happen with a plan or project you know about. Give your prediction and say how sure you are, and why. If they push you to sound more certain than your evidence allows, hold your ground politely.

lessons.check: What is the difference between 'the results prove' and 'the results indicate'? When would you use each?

lessons.title: Putting the weight where it belongs: cleft sentences
lessons.why: In an interview or a meeting, a cleft sentence tells the listener which part to remember.
lessons.rule: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two parts to point at what matters. 'What + clause + is + point' puts the point at the end: What we need is more time. 'It is/was + point + that + clause' puts it early: It was the client that asked for the change. Use them for your one key point, not in every sentence.

passage.title: Interview answer: 'What did you learn in your last role?'
passage.text:
What I learned most in my last role is that people rarely read long reports. When I joined, the team sent a twenty-page update to the board every month. It was the chair, in my first week, who told me she only ever read the first page.

So I changed the format. All the board needed was a concise summary: three decisions, two risks and one number that showed progress. The detail was still there in an appendix for anyone who wanted it.

The reason this mattered is that the board had been delaying decisions because they could not find what they were being asked. After the change, the average time to approve a proposal fell from six weeks to two.

I would argue that the lesson goes beyond reports. What people need from you is not everything you know, but the part that helps them act. It was that idea, more than any single skill, that I took into every project afterwards.

links.title: Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion and auxiliaries

drills.prompt: The interviewer thinks the problem was the budget. You want to correct them: it was the timeline. Which sentence does this best?
options: The timeline was a problem, and the budget was too.
It was the timeline that caused the problem, not the budget.
What caused the problem was the budget.
drills.hint: Which one points clearly at the timeline and away from the budget?
drills.why: The it-cleft puts 'the timeline' in focus and 'not the budget' corrects the listener. The first blurs the point; the third says the opposite.

drills.sentence: What worries me most ___ the lack of a clear owner.
drills.hint: The what-clause counts as one thing.
drills.why: A what-clause acts as a single subject, and 'the lack' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.

drills.sentence: It was the second test ___ showed the fault.
drills.hint: It-clefts have their own linking word.
drills.why: It-clefts use 'that' (or 'who' for people). 'What' belongs to the other kind of cleft.

drills.sentence: The reason we missed the deadline is because the data arrived late.
drills.answer: The reason we missed the deadline is that the data arrived late.
drills.hint: This is a formal report. Look at the word after 'is'.
drills.why: 'The reason ... is because' says 'reason' twice and is avoided in formal English. Use 'the reason ... is that'.

drills.answer: What we need is a concise summary.
drills.hint: Start with 'What' and keep the key point for the end.
drills.why: A what-cleft saves the important part, 'a concise summary', for the end, where the listener notices it.

answers: It was the client's change to the brief that caused the delay.
What caused the delay was the client's change to the brief.
It was the client changing the brief that caused the delay.
What caused the delay was that the client changed the brief.
drills.hint: Use a cleft sentence to point at the cause.
drills.why: A cleft sentence makes the cause the focus, so the listener knows exactly what you are blaming.

drills.answer: All we need is one more week.
drills.hint: 'All' here means 'the only thing'.
drills.why: An all-cleft says that this one thing is enough, which makes a request sound small and reasonable.

write.prompt: Answer this interview question in writing: 'Tell me about something you changed at work or in your studies.' Use at least one what-cleft, one it-cleft and one 'The reason ___ is that ___' to point at the parts you want the interviewer to remember.

speak.prompt: The interviewer asks what you learned from a difficult project. Answer with one clear point and mark it with a cleft sentence, such as 'What I learned was ...'. If you need a moment before the key point, take it: a pause often makes the point land harder.

lessons.check: Say one sentence about your work in two ways: once plainly and once as a cleft sentence. What changes for the listener?

lessons.title: Turning actions into ideas: nominalisation
lessons.why: Reports and formal writing pack actions into nouns, and learning to build and unpack them makes both your writing and your reading faster.
lessons.rule: Nominalisation turns a verb or adjective into a noun: 'prices increased' becomes 'the increase in prices'; 'we decided' becomes 'our decision'. The noun can then be the subject of a new sentence, which makes reports compact and formal. In speech and friendly emails, verbs are usually clearer. A participle clause ('Having reviewed the data, we ...') also packs two steps into one sentence, as long as both parts have the same subject.

passage.title: Report extract: staff turnover this year
passage.text:
Staff turnover rose from 11 to 18 per cent over the year. The increase in departures was concentrated in the first six months of service, which suggests that the problem lies in how new staff are brought in rather than in pay.

Having carried out a comprehensive review of exit interviews, we attribute most of the rise to two factors. The first is the reduction in training time, from four weeks to ten days, which was introduced to save money. The second is the removal of the buddy scheme, under which each new starter was paired with an experienced colleague.

The reduction in training led to a rise in errors during the first month, and several leavers described feeling 'thrown in'. The introduction of a shorter induction has therefore cost more than it saved, since the replacement of each leaver costs an estimated four thousand pounds.

The implication is clear. The restoration of both the full training period and the buddy scheme should be a priority for the coming year.

drills.prompt: Which sentence suits a formal report?
options: Prices went up a lot, so people bought less.
The sharp rise in prices led to a fall in demand.
Prices went up and demand, like, dropped.
drills.hint: Look for actions turned into nouns.
drills.why: 'The sharp rise in prices' and 'a fall in demand' are nominalisations, which give the compact, formal tone a report needs. The first is fine in conversation; the third is very casual.

drills.sentence: The ___ of the new system has reduced errors.
drills.hint: What kind of word comes between 'The' and 'of'?
drills.why: After 'The' and before 'of' you need a noun: 'the introduction of'.

drills.sentence: We ___ the fall in complaints to the new training.
drills.hint: Which verb follows the pattern 'X to Y'?
drills.why: You attribute a result to a cause. 'Indicate' and 'mitigate' do not take 'to' in this way.

answers: The sharp increase in prices led to a fall in demand.
The sharp increase in prices caused a fall in demand.
The sharp rise in prices led to a fall in demand.
The sharp rise in prices caused a fall in demand.
drills.hint: Turn both verbs into nouns and link them with 'led to'.
drills.why: 'Increased' becomes 'the increase in', 'fell' becomes 'a fall in', and 'led to' shows cause and effect in one formal sentence.

parts: We decided to restore the buddy scheme.
answers: Having reviewed the exit interviews, we decided to restore the buddy scheme.
After reviewing the exit interviews, we decided to restore the buddy scheme.
drills.hint: Both sentences have the same subject. Start with 'Having'.
drills.why: A perfect participle clause shows that the first action finished before the second, without repeating 'we'.

drills.sentence: Having reviewed the data, the decision was made to extend the trial.
drills.answer: Having reviewed the data, we decided to extend the trial.
accept: Having reviewed the data, we made the decision to extend the trial.
Having reviewed the data, the team decided to extend the trial.
drills.hint: Who reviewed the data?
drills.why: A participle clause takes the subject of the main clause. Here that is 'the decision', which cannot review anything, so the meaning goes wrong.

drills.answer: The delay in approval led to higher costs.
drills.hint: Start with the noun phrase for the cause.
drills.why: 'The delay in approval' is a nominalisation of 'approval was delayed', and it works as the subject of 'led to'.

write.prompt: Write a short report extract explaining a change and its effects in your workplace, your studies or your town. Use at least three nominalisations (the increase in, the introduction of, the decision to ...) and one 'Having ___' clause. Then read it again: if any sentence is so full of nouns that it is hard to follow, turn that one back into verbs.

speak.prompt: Say your report extract aloud as if presenting it at a meeting. Then say the same points as you would to a friend, using verbs instead of nouns. Notice which version suits which listener.

lessons.check: Turn 'We closed the office because costs rose' into a formal sentence using nouns. Which version would you use in a message to a friend, and why?

lessons.title: Following the thread: discourse markers and summaries
lessons.why: Markers like 'that said' and 'by contrast' tell you where an argument is going; if you notice them, you can summarise a complex text accurately.

passage.title: Research summary: a four-day week trial
passage.text:
Twenty-two organisations took part in a six-month trial of a four-day week, with no loss of pay. With regard to productivity, the results were broadly positive: most organisations reported that output stayed the same, and five reported a rise.

The staff survey tells a similar story. Reported stress fell in eighteen of the twenty-two organisations. By contrast, the effect on customer satisfaction was mixed, and two organisations with call centres found it hard to cover the fifth day.

There is also a discrepancy in the data that deserves attention. Managers reported fewer sick days, while the payroll records show almost no change. To put it another way, the improvement may be real, but we cannot yet confirm it from the records.

That said, nineteen organisations have chosen to continue with the four-day week. In light of this, the authors recommend a longer trial with independent measures of output.

To sum up, the trial suggests that a shorter week is feasible for many office-based employers, while services that must be open five days a week face harder choices.

drills.prompt: According to the summary, what happened to sick days?
options: Managers said they fell, but the payroll records do not confirm it.
They rose in the organisations with call centres.
drills.hint: Find the word 'discrepancy'.
drills.why: The text points to a discrepancy: two sources disagree, so the fall is reported but not confirmed.

drills.prompt: What does 'That said' do at the start of the fourth paragraph?
options: It adds a point that weighs against the doubt just raised.
It repeats the previous point in simpler words.
drills.hint: What came just before it, and does the next sentence agree or push back?
drills.why: 'That said' limits what came before. After the doubt about sick days, it adds a strong point on the other side: nineteen organisations are continuing.

drills.sentence: The budget is fixed. ___, we cannot hire anyone else this year.
drills.hint: The second sentence says the same thing in practical terms.
drills.why: 'To put it another way' restates a point more simply. There is no contrast, and 'with regard to' needs a noun after it.

drills.sentence: ___ the new figures, we have revised our forecast.
drills.hint: The figures are the reason for the change.
drills.why: 'In light of' means 'taking this into account' and is followed by a noun. The other two link whole sentences and do not show a reason.

drills.sentence: The trial proved that a shorter week is feasible for many office-based employers.
drills.answer: The trial suggests that a shorter week is feasible for many office-based employers.
accept: The trial indicates that a shorter week is feasible for many office-based employers.
drills.hint: Check the verb the writer uses in the last paragraph.
drills.why: An accurate summary keeps the writer's level of certainty. The text says 'suggests'; 'proved' overclaims.

answers: While stress fell in most organisations, customer satisfaction was mixed.
Although stress fell in most organisations, customer satisfaction was mixed.
Stress fell in most organisations, whereas customer satisfaction was mixed.
Stress fell in most organisations; by contrast, customer satisfaction was mixed.
drills.hint: Show that the two results point in different directions.
drills.why: 'While', 'although', 'whereas' or 'by contrast' tell the reader that the second fact is different from the first.

drills.answer: To sum up, the trial was largely positive.
drills.hint: Start with the marker that closes a text.
drills.why: 'To sum up' signals the conclusion, so the reader knows the main point is coming.

write.prompt: Take a report, article or study you have read recently (or use the passage above) and write a summary for a busy manager. Keep the writer's level of certainty, use at least three markers (that said, by contrast, in light of ...) to show how the points connect, and finish with 'To sum up'.

speak.prompt: A colleague missed the meeting where the four-day week results were presented. Summarise them for them: the main finding, one contrast, one doubt and the recommendation. If they ask 'So did it work or not?', answer honestly with the right amount of certainty.

lessons.check: What is the difference between 'that said' and 'to put it another way'? Say one sentence with each.

lessons.title: The interview: evidence, tone and hard questions
lessons.why: A strong answer does not need to be fast or smooth; it needs a clear story, evidence and the right tone for the room.

passage.title: Interview answer: 'Tell me about a time a project went wrong.'
passage.text:
That's a fair question, and I'd like to answer it with a real example.

To give you some context, I was part of a team moving a charity's donor records to a new database. We had a fixed launch date because a fundraising campaign depended on it. My role was to check that the data had been transferred correctly.

Two weeks before launch, I found that about three per cent of records had lost their contact preferences. That meant we might email people who had asked not to be contacted, which is a serious problem under data protection law.

I raised it with the project lead the same day and proposed a delay of one week, so that we could repair the records and test them properly. The delay may well have looked like a failure at the time, but it protected the charity from a much bigger one. As a result, the launch went ahead with no complaints, and the campaign raised slightly more than its target.

With hindsight, I would have tested a sample of records much earlier. I would argue that the real lesson was about timing: finding a problem is only useful if there is still room to fix it.

drills.prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Why should we believe you're good under pressure?' Which opening sets up an answer with evidence?
options: I'm just naturally good under pressure.
To give you some context, last spring our main supplier failed a week before a launch.
Everybody says I'm calm, so I must be.
drills.hint: Which one starts a real example?
drills.why: It begins a specific story, which the interviewer can believe. The other two are claims without evidence.

drills.sentence: ___, I would have asked for help sooner.
drills.hint: The speaker is looking back and saying what they would change.
drills.why: 'With hindsight' introduces what you would do differently now. 'As a result' reports an effect, and 'to give you some context' opens a story.

drills.sentence: My role ___ to check the data before launch.
drills.hint: The phrase is 'my role ___ to'.
drills.why: 'My role was to' plus a verb states your responsibility: the Task step of a STAR answer.

drills.prompt: You are ending a formal email to a new client. Which line fits?
options: Give me a shout if anything's unclear.
Please do not hesitate to contact me if anything is unclear.
drills.hint: You do not know this person well yet.
drills.why: A first formal email calls for 'Please do not hesitate to contact me'. The other two are friendly and fine with a colleague you know, but too casual here.

drills.sentence: With hindsight, the launch went ahead on time and the client renewed the contract.
drills.answer: As a result, the launch went ahead on time and the client renewed the contract.
drills.hint: This sentence reports what happened because of your action.
drills.why: 'With hindsight' introduces what you would do differently. The Result step of the answer needs 'As a result'.

parts: The delay looked bad at the time.
It protected the charity from a bigger problem.
answers: The delay may well have looked bad at the time, but it protected the charity from a bigger problem.
While the delay looked bad at the time, it protected the charity from a bigger problem.
Although the delay looked bad at the time, it protected the charity from a bigger problem.
drills.hint: Admit the first point, then give yours.
drills.why: Conceding a fair point first ('may well', 'while', 'although') makes your own point more convincing.

drills.answer: My role was to check the data.
drills.hint: Start with the phrase for your responsibility.
drills.why: In a STAR answer, 'My role was to' marks the Task step clearly.

drills.prompt: The interviewer says: 'Your project went over budget, didn't it?' Which reply handles the hard question best?
options: That's a fair question. It did, by eight per cent, and here is what we learned.
Budgets always go over, so it doesn't matter.
drills.hint: Look for honesty plus evidence.
drills.why: It accepts the question, gives an exact number and moves on to what was learned. Taking a moment before answering is fine too.

write.prompt: Write a structured report on a project you were part of, for a panel reviewing your application. Use the headings Context, My role, Actions, Results and Reflection. Support each claim with evidence (a number, a date or a concrete change), hedge where your evidence is limited, and keep the tone formal throughout.

speak.prompt: A hard interview for a job you want. The interviewer asks you to describe a project that went wrong, then challenges one of your claims. Answer with the context, your role, what you did and the result, and give evidence when pushed. Pauses, repeated sounds and time spent finding a word are all fine: what counts is that your story and your evidence come across.

lessons.check: Tell the story of one success using the four STAR steps. Which phrase did you use to open each step?

placement.prompt: Which sentence best suits a report based on one small study?
options: This study proves that the method works.
This study suggests that the method may be effective.
This study shows that the method definitely works.

placement.sentence: It was the finance team ___ spotted the error.
The ___ of the new policy led to fewer complaints.
